problems.stem: In Max Roser's *Short History of Global Living Conditions*, the share of the world living in extreme poverty roughly 200 years ago was approximately:

options.comment: Roser's number is much higher — nearly four in five people in 1820.
Too low; the framing depends on most of the world being in extreme poverty.
Still short of Roser's figure.
Correct. ~80% in 1820, under 10% today.

problems.solution: Roser's headline statistic: 200 years ago nearly $80\%$ of the world lived in extreme poverty; today the share is under $10\%$.

review.label: Roser, OWID — A history of global living conditions

problems.stem: A country grows at $3.5\%$ per year. Roughly how many years does it take real GDP per capita to double? Use the rule of 70.
problems.solution: The rule of 70: doubling time $\approx \frac{70}{g}$. Here $\frac{70}{3.5} = 20$ years.

problems.stem: In two or three sentences, explain why a $2\%$ vs. $4\%$ annual growth rate matters enormously over a human lifetime.
problems.model_answer: Compounding. At $2\%$ a country doubles in 35 years; at $4\%$ it doubles in about 17.5. Over an 80-year lifetime that's roughly two doublings vs. four-and-a-half — the difference between modest improvement and a transformed standard of living.
key_points: Rule of 70 applied to both rates.
Doubling is the lived-experience metric.
Several doublings over a lifetime is qualitatively different.

problems.stem: Coffee beans become more expensive. In the market for ground coffee at a shop, the most likely short-run effect is:

options.text: Demand shifts left
options.comment: Input prices hit sellers, not buyers.

options.text: Supply shifts left
options.comment: Correct. Higher input costs shift supply up and to the left.

options.text: Quantity demanded rises
options.comment: Quantity demanded falls along the new equilibrium.

options.text: Equilibrium price falls
options.comment: Price rises, not falls.

problems.solution: An input-price increase is a leftward shift of supply. New equilibrium: higher price, lower quantity.

problems.stem: True or false: A binding price ceiling set above the equilibrium price produces a shortage.

options.text: True
options.comment: A ceiling above equilibrium isn't binding.

options.text: False
options.comment: Correct. Only ceilings below equilibrium produce shortages.

problems.solution: Only ceilings *below* equilibrium are binding. Above equilibrium, the market clears as if the ceiling weren't there.

problems.stem: Demand for chai is $Q_d = 80 - 4P$ and supply is $Q_s = 20 + 2P$. What is the equilibrium price?
Which of the following is a *positive* (not normative) statement?

options.text: The minimum wage should be raised
options.comment: "Should" makes this normative.

options.text: Raising the minimum wage reduces employment among low-skill workers
options.comment: Correct. Empirical claim about how the world is.

options.text: It is unfair that some people earn far more than others
options.comment: "Unfair" is a value judgment — normative.

options.text: The government ought to fight inflation aggressively
options.comment: "Ought" makes this normative.

problems.solution: *Positive* statements describe how the world *is* — they can be tested against data. *Normative* statements describe how it *ought to be* — they involve value judgments. "Should," "ought," "fair," and "unfair" are markers of normative claims.

problems.stem: Explain *ceteris paribus* in two sentences and give one example of how economists use it.
problems.model_answer: *Ceteris paribus* means "holding other things equal" — it lets economists isolate the effect of one variable by assuming everything else stays constant. For example, the demand curve plots quantity demanded vs. price *ceteris paribus*: income, tastes, and the price of related goods are all held fixed so we can see the pure price effect.
key_points: Definition: holding other things equal.
Used to isolate one variable's effect.
Concrete example with another variable held fixed.

problems.stem: A per-unit tax is imposed on sellers of a good. Compared to the no-tax outcome, the new equilibrium has:

options.text: Higher price paid by buyers, higher quantity sold
options.comment: Quantity falls with a tax.

options.text: Higher price paid by buyers, lower quantity sold
options.comment: Correct. The tax wedges the buyer price above the seller price.

options.text: Lower price paid by buyers, higher quantity sold
options.comment: Buyers pay more, not less.

options.text: No change in price; only the seller's profit falls
options.comment: Tax incidence splits between sides based on elasticities.

problems.solution: A tax creates a wedge: buyers pay $P_b$, sellers receive $P_s = P_b - t$. Quantity falls to where buyers' willingness to pay equals sellers' willingness to accept *plus the tax*.

problems.stem: A city imposes a \$1 per-gallon excise tax on gasoline. In two or three sentences, explain who bears the larger share of the tax burden and what determines that split.
problems.model_answer: The side with the *less elastic* curve bears the larger share, because they can't easily substitute away. Short-run gasoline demand is relatively inelastic, so buyers bear most of the \$1 tax. The split would shift toward sellers if buyers had readier substitutes (public transit, electric vehicles).
key_points: Tax incidence is determined by relative elasticities.
More inelastic side bears the larger share.
Short-run gasoline demand is inelastic, so buyers bear most of the burden.

problems.stem: Use a supply-and-demand diagram and prose to explain why a binding price floor (e.g., a minimum wage above the market wage) produces deadweight loss. Identify who gains, who loses, and the social efficiency cost.
problems.model_answer:
A binding price floor sits above the equilibrium price, so quantity demanded falls below quantity supplied — a surplus. In the labor market under a minimum wage, that surplus is *unemployment*: more workers want jobs at the wage floor than employers want to hire.

Winners: workers who keep their jobs and earn the higher wage. Losers: workers who would have been hired at the market wage but are not at the floor (the surplus labor), plus employers who pay more for the workers they retain. Deadweight loss is the surplus from foregone hires — those whose marginal value to the employer was above the equilibrium wage but below the floor.

The efficiency cost is the value of the trades that no longer happen. Distributional gains to retained workers can be substantial, which is why minimum wage policy is a debate about trade-offs, not a simple efficiency question.
key_points: Binding floor → quantity supplied > quantity demanded.
In labor markets, that surplus is unemployment.
Winners: retained workers. Losers: unhired workers, employers.
DWL = value of foregone trades.
Acknowledge distributional trade-off, not pure inefficiency story.

problems.stem: Country A produces 10 cars or 100 wheat per worker. Country B produces 5 cars or 80 wheat per worker. Comparative advantage in wheat belongs to:

options.text: Country A, because it has higher absolute productivity in both
options.comment: Absolute productivity doesn't determine comparative advantage.

options.text: Country B, because its opportunity cost of wheat is lower
options.comment: Correct. B gives up $5/80 = 0.0625$ cars per bushel; A gives up $10/100 = 0.10$.

options.text: Neither — they have identical opportunity costs
options.comment: They differ: 0.10 vs 0.0625.

options.text: Cannot be determined without prices
options.comment: Comparative advantage is defined from production possibilities alone.

problems.solution: Comparative advantage goes to whoever has the *lower opportunity cost*. B's opportunity cost of one bushel of wheat is $\frac{5}{80} = 0.0625$ cars; A's is $\frac{10}{100} = 0.10$. B specializes in wheat, A in cars; both gain.

problems.stem: Suppose one country can make either 60 widgets or 30 gizmos in a day. The opportunity cost of one gizmo, in widgets, is:
problems.solution: Trading one gizmo means giving up the chance to make widgets in that time. With 60 widgets or 30 gizmos available, one gizmo costs $\frac{60}{30} = 2$ widgets.

problems.stem: A country imposes a tariff on imported sugar. In two or three sentences, identify the main winners and losers.
problems.model_answer: Winners: domestic sugar producers (who face less foreign competition and sell at a higher price) and the government (which collects tariff revenue). Losers: domestic sugar consumers (paying more), and foreign sugar producers (losing market share). Net welfare typically falls — the consumer loss exceeds the producer-plus-government gain, leaving deadweight loss.
key_points: Winners: domestic producers + government revenue.
Losers: domestic consumers + foreign producers.
Net deadweight loss is the standard result.

problems.stem: Which of the following is most clearly a *market failure* (not just a market outcome someone dislikes)?

options.text: A new restaurant fails because it can't attract customers
options.comment: That's a market *working* — bad products lose.

options.text: A factory pollutes the river downstream without paying for the damage
options.comment: Correct. An uninternalized externality is a textbook market failure.

options.text: Some workers earn far more than others
options.comment: Inequality is a distributional outcome, not a failure of market mechanics.

options.text: Gas prices rise after a hurricane
options.comment: Prices adjusting to scarcity is markets working.

problems.solution: Market failure means the private market produces an inefficient outcome that an idealized market wouldn't. Externalities, public goods, monopoly power, and asymmetric information are the classic four. Disliking distributional outcomes or short-run price moves isn't the same thing.

problems.stem: Which of these is *not* counted in GDP?

options.text: A barbershop haircut
options.comment: Final services count.

options.text: A new car bought by a household
options.comment: Final consumption counts.

options.text: A used car bought by a household
options.comment: Correct. Used goods aren't new production this period.

options.text: A new washing machine sold to a household
options.comment: Final consumption counts.

problems.solution: GDP measures the value of *new* final goods and services produced in a period. Used goods were already counted when first produced. Counting them again would double-count.

problems.stem: Nominal GDP grew from \$20 trillion to \$22 trillion. The GDP deflator rose from 100 to 105. What was the approximate percent change in real GDP? Round to one decimal.
problems.solution: Real GDP$_t = \frac{\text{Nominal}_t}{\text{Deflator}_t} \times 100$. Year 0: $20$. Year 1: $\frac{22}{105} \times 100 \approx 20.95$. Percent change: $\frac{20.95-20}{20} \approx 4.76\%$, rounding to $4.8\%$. Quick check: nominal $10\%$ minus inflation $5\%$ $\approx 5\%$.

problems.stem: Briefly explain why the unemployment rate can fall even when no new jobs are created.
problems.model_answer: The unemployment rate is the ratio of unemployed people to the labor force. If discouraged workers stop looking for work, they leave the labor force entirely and are no longer counted as unemployed. The numerator and denominator both fall — and because the numerator falls by more in percentage terms, the unemployment rate goes down without any new hiring.
key_points: Rate = unemployed / labor force.
Leaving the labor force removes you from both numerator and denominator.
No new jobs needed for the rate to drop.

problems.stem: In the Solow framework, in the absence of technological progress a country's long-run growth in real GDP *per worker*:

options.text: Continues indefinitely as capital accumulates
options.comment: Ignores diminishing returns.

options.text: Approaches zero at the steady state
options.comment: Correct. Diminishing returns to capital drive per-worker growth to zero at the steady state.

options.text: Equals the savings rate
options.comment: Savings rate determines the *level*, not the long-run growth rate.

options.text: Equals the population growth rate
options.comment: Total GDP grows with population; per-worker GDP doesn't.

problems.solution: The Solow model's central insight: capital exhibits diminishing returns. Without technological progress, accumulation alone can't sustain per-worker growth — it approaches zero. Sustained per-worker growth requires technology.

problems.stem: Why have some countries (e.g., South Korea) grown roughly 40-fold since 1900 while others (e.g., Niger) have barely grown at all? Identify the standard growth-economics factors and explain which seem most decisive in cross-country comparisons.
problems.model_answer:
Standard growth accounting points to three proximate factors: physical capital per worker, human capital (education, skills, health), and total factor productivity (TFP) — the residual that captures technology, organization, and how efficiently inputs are combined.

In cross-country comparisons, TFP differences explain most of the variation in income levels. Physical-capital differences matter but are second-order; you can buy machines, build factories, and copy technology. What's harder to copy is the *institutional* environment that makes investment, education, and innovation pay off: secure property rights, contract enforcement, low corruption, openness to trade and ideas, functioning capital markets.

The deeper-cause literature (Acemoglu–Robinson, North) traces TFP differences back to institutions. South Korea adopted policies and built institutions that rewarded productive investment after 1960; Niger has faced political instability, weak property rights, and limited integration with global markets. The lesson: capital and education are channels; institutions are the bedrock.
key_points: Three proximate factors: physical capital, human capital, TFP.
TFP explains most cross-country variation in income.
Institutions (property rights, rule of law, openness) are the deepest cause.
Concrete contrast: South Korea's institutional shift vs. Niger's instability.
Capital and education are channels; institutions enable them.

problems.unit_title: Money, the Fed, and Exchange Rates
problems.stem: The Fed conducts an open-market *purchase* of Treasury securities. The most direct first-round effect is:

options.text: Bank reserves rise; federal funds rate falls
options.comment: Correct. Adding reserves pushes the funds rate down.

options.text: Bank reserves fall; federal funds rate rises
options.comment: That's an open-market *sale* — opposite operation.

options.text: The money multiplier falls
options.comment: OMOs don't change the multiplier mechanically.

options.text: The required reserve ratio falls
options.comment: Reserve requirements are set administratively, not by OMOs.

problems.solution: An open-market purchase credits sellers' accounts with new reserves. More reserves in the overnight market push the federal funds rate down toward the policy target. This is the transmission's first link.

problems.unit_title: Money, the Fed, and Exchange Rates
problems.stem: Briefly explain why doubling the money supply doesn't (in the long run) double real GDP.
problems.model_answer: Money is a unit of account and medium of exchange — doubling it changes the *nominal* scale of prices and wages, not the *real* quantity of goods produced. In the long run, doubling $M$ roughly doubles the price level $P$, leaving $\frac{M}{P}$ (real balances) and real GDP essentially unchanged. This is the long-run neutrality of money — and the basis for the quantity theory: $MV = PY$.
key_points: Money is a numéraire, not a real input.
Long-run neutrality: $M \uparrow$ shifts $P$, not $Y$.
Connect to $MV = PY$.

problems.stem: Which of the following would shift the AD curve to the *right*?

options.text: A rise in oil prices that raises production costs
options.comment: That shifts SRAS, not AD.

options.text: A federal tax cut for households
options.comment: Correct. Higher disposable income raises consumption — AD shifts right.

options.text: An increase in the reserve requirement
options.comment: That's contractionary — AD shifts left.

options.text: A drought that reduces agricultural output
options.comment: Supply shock — affects SRAS, not AD.

problems.solution: AD shifters: consumption, investment, government spending, net exports, expectations, monetary/fiscal policy. A tax cut for households raises disposable income → higher C → AD right.

problems.stem: Use AS/AD to explain *stagflation* — simultaneously rising inflation and rising unemployment. Identify which curve shifts and why this pattern was hard to reconcile with the pre-1970s Phillips curve view.
problems.model_answer:
Stagflation is a *leftward shift of short-run aggregate supply (SRAS)*. The classic 1970s case was the oil shock: input prices rose sharply, shifting SRAS up and to the left. With AD roughly unchanged, the new equilibrium sat at a higher price level *and* lower real GDP — inflation and unemployment rising together.

The pre-1970s Phillips curve view treated inflation and unemployment as inversely related along a stable trade-off. Stagflation broke that intuition because it involved supply-side dynamics, not demand-side movement along a fixed curve. Friedman and Phelps had already argued the long-run Phillips curve was vertical at the natural rate — the 1970s validated that view.

Lesson: demand-side stimulus doesn't cure a supply-side shock. Output gaps from SRAS shifts call for different remedies than those from AD shifts.
key_points: Stagflation = SRAS leftward shift, not movement along AD.
Result: higher price level AND lower real GDP simultaneously.
Pre-1970s Phillips view assumed stable inflation-unemployment trade-off.
Friedman-Phelps long-run vertical Phillips curve vindicated.
Policy implication: demand stimulus doesn't fix supply shocks.

problems.stem: An *automatic stabilizer* is best described as:

options.text: A discretionary spending bill passed in response to a recession
options.comment: That's discretionary fiscal policy, not automatic.

options.text: A budget feature that expands the deficit in recessions and contracts it in expansions without new legislation
options.comment: Correct. Unemployment insurance and progressive income tax are the standard examples.

options.text: A Federal Reserve rule for setting interest rates
options.comment: That's a monetary policy rule, not fiscal.

options.text: A constitutional balanced-budget requirement
options.comment: That would prevent automatic stabilizers from working.

problems.solution: Automatic stabilizers respond to the cycle through existing programs — UI payouts rise when unemployment rises, tax receipts fall when incomes fall. They smooth without requiring new acts of Congress, which gives them a faster (if smaller) response than discretionary policy.

problems.stem: Distinguish *automatic stabilizers* from *discretionary fiscal policy* in two or three sentences, with one example of each.
problems.model_answer: Automatic stabilizers adjust to the business cycle *without* new legislation — unemployment insurance pays out more in recessions, progressive income tax receipts fall when incomes fall. Discretionary fiscal policy requires a new act of Congress — the 2009 ARRA stimulus or the 2020 CARES Act. Automatic stabilizers respond faster but are smaller; discretionary changes can be larger but face implementation lags.
key_points: Automatic stabilizers operate without new legislation.
Discretionary fiscal policy requires new legislation.
Examples: UI / progressive tax (auto); ARRA / CARES (discretionary).
Bonus: speed vs. magnitude trade-off.

flashcards.definition: The value of the next-best alternative given up when a choice is made.
flashcards.why: The only cost concept that consistently shows up in real decisions — money, time, attention. If you don't compare alternatives, you're not doing economics.

flashcards.definition: *Nominal* is measured in current-period prices. *Real* is adjusted for the price level, expressed in base-period prices. $\text{Real} = \frac{\text{Nominal}}{\text{Price index}} \times 100$.
flashcards.why: Comparing nominal values across time or countries is almost always misleading. Real values are what answer 'is this actually more?'

flashcards.definition: Doubling time in years $\approx \frac{70}{g}$, where $g$ is annual growth in percent.
flashcards.why: Converts growth rates to lived-experience timescales. 2% doubles in 35 years; 7% doubles in 10. The difference between Argentina and South Korea.

flashcards.definition: Vertical at the economy's potential output. In the long run, prices and wages adjust so output returns to potential regardless of the price level.
flashcards.why: The anchor for what 'normal' looks like. Short-run movements are deviations from this vertical line; policy can only push you off it temporarily.

flashcards.definition: $M \times V = P \times Y$. With $V$ and $Y$ roughly stable in the long run, changes in $M$ translate into changes in $P$.
flashcards.why: The first thing to reach for when asked 'why does inflation happen?' Long-run inflation is a monetary phenomenon.

flashcards.definition: A producer has a comparative advantage in a good if its *opportunity cost* of producing that good is lower than the other producer's.
flashcards.why: Trade is mutually beneficial whenever comparative advantages differ — even if one side is absolutely better at everything. The pattern, not the levels, drives gains.
